title: Image Classifier App: From Data to Mobile
description: Build a complete mobile‑ready image classifier using transfer learning, TFLite, and the Task Library.
problemStatement:
## Scenario
You are an ML engineer at a startup that wants to build an app to identify **flower species** (daisy, dandelion, roses, sunflowers, tulips) from a smartphone camera.

## Your Mission
Create an end‑to‑end pipeline that:
- Loads and processes a dataset of flower images.
- Fine‑tunes a pre‑trained MobileNetV2 model.
- Applies quantization‑aware training (QAT) for mobile efficiency.
- Converts the model to TensorFlow Lite with metadata.
- Writes a client‑side inference code snippet (Android/Kotlin) using the TFLite Task Library.

You will **combine everything** from this course: data pipelines with `tf.data`, transfer learning, fine‑tuning, QAT, TFLite conversion, and mobile integration.

## Dataset
The project uses the TF Flowers dataset (or you can create a synthetic substitute). The dataset contains 3,670 images of 5 flower classes, split into training and validation.

## Deliverables
1. A Jupyter notebook (or Python script) that performs the full training‑to‑conversion workflow.
2. A `.tflite` file with metadata (at minimum, the model file).
3. The key metrics: final test accuracy, TFLite model size, and average inference latency on a batch of images.
4. A short Kotlin code snippet showing how to use the produced `.tflite` file in an Android app.
requirements: Use `tf.keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory` (or `tf.data` with file paths) to load and preprocess the dataset.
Apply data augmentation (RandomFlip, RandomRotation) as part of the model or the input pipeline.
Build the model with a frozen MobileNetV2 base and a custom classifier head (GlobalAveragePooling + Dropout + Dense).
Fine‑tune the top 20% of the base layers with a very low learning rate (≤1e-5).
Apply quantization‑aware training (QAT) using the TensorFlow Model Optimization Toolkit and train for at least 2 additional epochs.
Convert the QAT model to TFLite with dynamic‑range quantization (`tf.lite.Optimize.DEFAULT`).
Add metadata (labels, normalization) to the TFLite file using the Metadata Writer API (optional but recommended).
Evaluate the TFLite model with a `tf.lite.Interpreter` on the test set and report the accuracy, file size, and average inference time.
Write a Kotlin `classifyImage()` function that uses `ImageClassifier.createFromFile` from the TFLite Task Library to return the top‑1 prediction.
hints: Use `tf.keras.applications.mobilenet_v2.preprocess_input` as a Lambda layer (or inside a map function) to normalize inputs.
To fine‑tune, unfreeze the base, then freeze all layers except the last 20% using `for layer in base_model.layers[:-int(len(base_model.layers)*0.2)]: layer.trainable = False`.
The TFLite Metadata Writer can be installed via `pip install tflite-support`. Follow the official guide to attach labels and normalization parameters.
For measuring inference time, use `time.perf_counter()` over many runs and remove warmup iterations.
The Kotlin Task Library dependency is `org.tensorflow:tensorflow-lite-task-vision`.
expectedOutput:
A complete Python script that trains, converts, and evaluates the model, outputting:
- Test accuracy of the final TFLite model (≥ 75% on the flowers dataset, or reasonable performance on synthetic data).
- TFLite file size (≤ 5 MB).
- Average inference time per image (≤ 50 ms on a typical CPU).
- The Kotlin function for mobile classification.
